rv.q: This piece has neither the formative ambition nor the acerbic core of "August: Osage County," which preceded "Donuts" at the Music Box Theatre. (Letts is the rare American playwright who gets to follow his own play in the same Broadway theater).

“Superior Donuts,” a gentle comedy that unfolds like an extended episode of a 1970s sitcom, is a warm bath of a play that will leave Broadway audiences with satisfied smiles rather than rattled nerves.

When a theater critic calls a play a sitcom, it's usually meant as a rap on the knuckles. But let's make an exception in the case of "Superior Donuts," the bracingly funny new play by Tracy Letts, and compare the work in a complimentary way to one of those Golden Age 1970s television comedies by Norman Lear — character-centered, socially and pol...

cn.t: Letts' softer follow-up to "August: Osage County" earns praise as warmhearted and entertaining, though critics note its formulaic, sitcom-like plotting. A charming but not groundbreaking crowd-pleaser.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
